opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is that you can't judge reasoning by looking at performance on a task in isolation, because almost any task can be solved without reasoning if you have enough prior knowledge or enough training data. If you've seen the problem before, or something very close to it, you can just retrieve the answer, or retrieve a program that solves it, and that looks exactly like reasoning from the outside. So skill on its own tells you very little. What you actually want to measure is how efficiently the system turns the information it has into the ability to handle situations it hasn't seen.

So the way I'd frame it is: reasoning ability, or intelligence more broadly, is about skill-acquisition efficiency. You have to control for two things. First, priors, meaning what knowledge was built into the system before it ever saw the task. Second, experience, meaning how much data or practice it got on that kind of task. If a model performs well, but it was trained on millions of examples that cover the test distribution, that's not evidence of reasoning, that's evidence of memorization and interpolation. Very useful, but a different thing.

In practice, that means a good evaluation of reasoning has to feature genuine novelty. The test problems should be things the system could not have anticipated, that can't be solved by pattern-matching against something in the training set, and ideally that a human with only basic core knowledge, like objectness, basic geometry, counting, could solve with just a few examples. That was the whole idea behind ARC. Every task is new, you get a handful of demonstrations, and you have to infer the underlying rule and apply it. You can't brute-force it with scale alone, at least not in principle, because the space of tasks is open-ended.

And I'd add one more thing: you also want to look at how the model gets to the answer, not just whether it gets it right. Does it actually construct a new program on the fly, adapted to the problem in front of it, or is it just fetching something stored? A system that reasons should be able to recombine what it knows to deal with something genuinely unfamiliar, and it should degrade gracefully as problems get further from what it's seen. If performance collapses the moment you shift the distribution a little, that's a strong signal it wasn't really reasoning in the first place.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning should be evaluated by how the system performs on novel situations and how it reaches answers, so it assesses the model through its behavior.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that a model’s quality depends on the goal it is intended to serve.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify simplicity or retaining causal factors as criteria for choosing a model.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that you can't judge reasoning by looking at performance on tasks the model has already seen, or tasks that are very similar to what it has seen. That's the fundamental mistake people keep making. If you train a model on millions of examples of a certain kind of problem, and then it solves another instance of that same kind of problem, that tells you almost nothing about reasoning. It tells you about memorization, about pattern matching, about the ability to retrieve and recombine templates. Which is useful! But it's not reasoning.

So the way I think about it is in terms of skill acquisition efficiency. Reasoning, in my view, is the ability to synthesize a new program, a new model, on the fly, when you encounter a situation you've never seen before, using very little data. The thing you want to measure is: how much novelty can the system handle, and how efficiently does it adapt to it? What's the ratio between what it already knew and what it can now do? That's intelligence. Intelligence is not skill. Skill is the output of intelligence. If you just measure skill, you're measuring something that can be bought with data and compute, and you can't tell whether there's any actual generalization happening underneath.

This is why I designed ARC the way I did. Each task is novel, each task should be solvable by a human with no special training, and crucially, you only get a couple of examples. You can't brute-force it with scale alone, because the tasks are not in the training distribution, and we deliberately try to keep them out. So when a system does well on ARC, you learn something meaningful: it was able to build a new model of a problem it had never encountered.

And I'd add a second criterion, which is that a good reasoner should be able to tell you why. Reasoning produces something you can inspect, a chain of steps, a program, a causal story. If the output is right but there's no legible process behind it, you should be suspicious that you're looking at interpolation rather than reasoning. The two can look identical from the outside on familiar problems, and they come apart completely the moment you step outside the training distribution. So judge the model on the edge of the distribution, not the center. That's where reasoning actually lives.

r001.rationale: The response says to judge reasoning by how the model performs on novel tasks and adapts to them, making its behavior the basis of assessment.

r002.rationale: It discusses measuring reasoning and intelligence but does not say that a model’s quality depends on the goal it is meant to serve.

r003.rationale: It mentions synthesizing a new model and producing an inspectable process, but does not propose choosing the simplest model that retains the causal factors needed for a goal.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to look at what happens when the model encounters a situation it hasn’t seen before. Getting the right answer to a familiar problem doesn’t tell you very much about reasoning, because that answer could come from memorizing a solution or recognizing a familiar template.

A good model should capture something about the underlying structure of the problem. You should be able to change the surface details, or introduce a new combination of constraints, and still use that model to work out what follows. So the question is: does it generalize beyond the examples that went into constructing it?

And you have to be careful about what you mean by novelty. Something can be new to your benchmark and still be very familiar to the system from training. Ideally, you want to control what experience the system has had, then test whether it can use that experience to solve problems that require a new adaptation. That’s much stronger evidence of reasoning than performance on a collection of familiar tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning should be judged by how the model behaves on unseen situations and whether it can generalize to new constraints.

r002.rationale: It discusses assessing reasoning and generalization, but does not say model quality depends on the goal it is intended to serve.

r003.rationale: It does not identify simplicity or retaining necessary causal factors as criteria for choosing a model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to look at what happens when you change the problem. If a model succeeds on something very close to what it has seen before, that doesn’t tell you very much about whether it can reason. It may simply be retrieving a familiar solution, even if that solution looks very sophisticated.

A stronger test is to give it a genuinely novel situation where the relevant information is available, but the solution has to be constructed. Can it identify the underlying structure, combine the things it knows, and adapt when you change an assumption? Does its approach still work when you remove the superficial cues?

So I would judge it primarily by generalization: how reliably it can handle new problems, and how much prior experience it needs to do so. A convincing explanation is useful, but it’s not sufficient. What matters is whether the model actually produces correct solutions under those changes.

r001.rationale: It says reasoning should be judged by what the model does on changed and novel problems, including whether it produces correct solutions.

r002.rationale: It discusses generalization as a way to assess reasoning but does not say model quality depends on the goal the model is intended to serve.

r003.rationale: It does not recommend the simplest model retaining the causal factors needed to achieve a goal.
